extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics; readers of classical geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and exposition of foundational principles, methods, and standard propositions in pre-Euclidean and Aristotelian mathematics (including spherical geometry and mechanics). Emphasises what counted as axioms, definitions, postulates, acceptable proofs, and common textbook practice in the Greek tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of first principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between axioms (common to all sciences), definitions, hypotheses and postulates (which differ for different sciences since they relate to the subject-matter of the particular science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle gives the clearest distinctions: axioms are 'common notions' (e.g. subtraction of equals), postulates are assumptions specific to the subject, definitions specify terms without asserting existence. Use this taxonomy when formulating foundational premises for a mathematical discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms versus postulates (Euclidean postulates as author's own)
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's axioms (common notions) are distinct from his postulates (constructions such as drawing lines and circles). The text infers Euclid himself formulated the postulates (including the 5th).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or reconstructing pre-Euclidean texts, treat Euclid's Postulates 1–5 as specific constructive assumptions rather than universal axioms; note especially the role of the 5th (parallel postulate) in avoiding circular reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions do not assert existence
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Aristotle, definitions only require to be understood; they do not assert existence or non-existence, except for unit/monad and magnitude whose existence must be assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mathematical exposition, separate definitional stipulation from existential claims; assume points and lines exist for geometry but prove existence of complex constructions by explicit construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction as proof of existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual construction (drawing/producing straight lines and circles) is the proof of existence in geometry; constructions (Postulates 1–3) serve as existence assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a theorem requires the existence of a figure, provide an explicit construction rather than merely asserting it. Treat construction steps as part of the logical proof of existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of petitio principii in foundational proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle criticises earlier treatments that assumed as hypotheses the very general propositions needed to prove elementary theorems (e.g., equality of angles in semicircles), thereby committing petitio principii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proofs do not presuppose the general result they aim to prove; introduce necessary postulates explicitly (Euclid's Postulate 5 is an example) rather than smuggling them into auxiliary assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion and use of the infinite (Eudoxus' lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle reports the method of exhaustion (Eudoxus' lemma) — continually adding or subtracting finite magnitudes to exceed or fall short of any assigned magnitude — and debates its relation to the 'infinite'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the lemma's heuristic role: mathematicians may use potential/instrumental notions of the infinite in proofs (method of exhaustion) without committing to actual infinites; archimedean-style justification was later given to legitimize such use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the continuous and the infinite (Aristotelian standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuous cannot be made up of indivisible parts; the infinite exists only potentially (not actually), and 'infinite' means always having something outside it rather than being without exterior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In foundational reasoning, treat continuity as a relation of touching parts with a single common boundary, and treat infinity as potential (processual) rather than an actually completed magnitude; this affects permissible proof techniques and philosophical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for acceptable proof-method differences (pre-Euclidean vs Euclidean)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's citations show earlier proofs sometimes relied on mixed angles or on assumptions equivalent to the target theorem; Euclid introduced different methods and order that removed such circularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical proofs or reconstructing methods, note whether arguments depend on ad-hoc or stronger assumptions; prefer methods that minimize hidden assumptions and avoid superfluous hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical structure of a Greek geometrical proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical form: a general enunciation, a particular enunciation with a labelled figure, the demonstration, and sometimes a concluding statement in words similar to the enunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this four-part format when presenting classical-style propositions for clarity and historical fidelity: (1) state the general claim, (2) restate with figure, (3) give the proof, (4) conclude explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook practice: acceptance of certain propositions without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Autolycus and others use a number of spherical propositions without proof or citation of authority, indicating an existing elementary textbook tradition for the sphere (later reflected in Theodosius's Sphaerica).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that some propositions were treated as standard (lemmas) in the tradition; when reconstructing or critiquing ancient texts, identify which results are invoked as 'known' and which are proved ab initio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram of velocities (mechanical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body has two linear movements in a constant ratio, its resultant path is a straight line given by the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by those movements; if the ratio varies, the path is a curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the parallelogram construction to resolve simultaneous linear motions; highlight that constancy of component ratio is the condition for straight-line resultant motion and varying ratio yields curved trajectories (ancient kinematic criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the lever and proportionality of mechanical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The moving weight relates inversely to the distances from the fulcrum ('as the weight moved is to the moving weight, so is the length to the length inversely'); greater distance corresponds to greater velocity in equal time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mechanical reasoning in terms of proportionalities of weights and lever arms and of distances described in equal times; these proportionalities underpin lever and balance arguments in Aristotelian/Mechanica accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram of forces derived from velocities and axioms of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: From the parallelogram of velocities and the axiom that force is proportional to distance described in given time, one obtains the parallelogram law for forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing ancient mechanics, derive force-composition rules from kinematic parallelograms combined with stated axioms about forces and distances; do not assume modern vector formalism without mapping ancient concepts onto it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of indivisible lines (consistency of foundational hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tract On Indivisible Lines (likely post-Aristotelian school) argues against the hypothesis that lines are composed of indivisible elements, claiming such hypotheses conflict with assumed mathematical principles and lead to contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate foundational proposals (like indivisibles) against the prevailing mathematical principles of the tradition; if a hypothesis forces contradiction with basic constructive or proportional principles, it should be rejected or reformulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-Euclidean standard propositions cited by Aristotle
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle records several substantive propositions not found in Euclid (but known earlier): (1) exterior angles of any polygon sum to four right angles; (2) locus with distances in a given ratio is a circle; (3) of closed lines with given area the circle has least circumference; (4) only two solids can fill space (pyramid and cube).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as examples of established geometric knowledge in the pre-Euclidean tradition; they indicate the scope of mathematical concerns (loci, isoperimetry, packing/filling) and can be used as benchmark results when comparing schools or tracing provenance of theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sphere and terminology usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle defines a sphere as the figure having all its radii equal (versus Euclid's later definition of the solid generated by revolving a semicircle); terms like 'axis' were not yet fully technical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing ancient sources, be attentive that definitions may be phrased differently (intensional vs generative) and that terminology (e.g., 'axis') may carry looser meaning than in later formal texts; prefer contextual reading.
